abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor-natural killer (CAR-NK) cells combine innate cytotoxicity with antigen-directed killing and promise as an immunotherapy with lower cytokine toxicity than CAR-T approaches. However, clinical translation is limited by challenges in transduction, persistence, tumor infiltration, and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). We performed a comprehensive literature review of recent preclinical and early-phase clinical studies, engineering strategies (CAR design, transduction technologies, gene-editing), manufacturing and expansion protocols, and trial outcomes in this review. We noted a reference to the advantages of CAR-NK, like multimodal killing (CAR-dependent and innate pathways), potential for allogeneic "off-the-shelf" use, and favorable early safety profiles. However, NK-specific obstacles persist: lower viral transduction efficiencies, short in vivo persistence, poor infiltration into solid tumors, and TME-mediated suppression (TGF-β, adenosine, metabolic stress). Engineering countermeasures such as IL-15 expression, checkpoint receptor knockout, chemokine receptor co-expression (e.g., CXCR1/4), DAP10/DAP12-based signaling domains, and non-viral delivery (transposons/CRISPR) have shown preclinical promise. CAR-NK therapy has developed from concept to a clinically actionable treatment line for hematologic malignancies and shows emerging potential in solid tumors when combined with TME-modulating strategies. This review provides robust evidence about CAR-NK therapies in hematological and solid tumors, with a great emphasis on the challenges they encounter, strategies, and innovative approaches to overcome these challenges, and forward-looking perspectives to improve future therapeutic CAR-NK designs and clinical outcomes.

abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the deadliest malignancies. Dysregulated RNA splicing has emerged as a critical mechanism contributing to PDAC progression. However, whether structural components of the spliceosome regulate oncogenic alternative splicing was not known. Here, we identify the nineteen complex (NTC) component BCAS2/SPF27 as a critical regulator of PDAC progression. Elevated expression of BCAS2 in PDAC is associated with poor patient outcomes. Transcriptomic analyses revealed that BCAS2 specifically regulates alternative exons with weak splice sites. In particular, BCAS2 promotes SOS1 exon 21 inclusion and consequently RAC-signaling activation. Furthermore, splice-switching antisense oligonucleotide (ASO)-mediated skipping of SOS1 exon 21 suppressed PDAC proliferation and migration. Our findings uncover a role of BCAS2 in the regulation of weak splice-site usage and identify the BCAS2-SOS1-RAC signaling axis as a potential therapeutic vulnerability in pancreatic cancer.

abstract: Therapeutic siRNAs are a major clinical modality for hepatic gene silencing, but efficient extrahepatic delivery and multi-gene modulation remain significant barriers. Nucleic acid nanotechnology offers programmable assembly, but conventional structures suffer from enzymatic instability in vivo . Here we report fully chemically modified RNA nanostructures (FMRNs)-a vehicle-free platform entirely composed of stabilized therapeutic nucleic acids that integrate structural precision with metabolic durability. Following systemic administration, FMRNs exhibit enhanced pharmacokinetics and extrahepatic accumulation, with in vivo behavior influenced greatly by hydrodynamic size rather than molecular weight. Using triangular and square geometries, we demonstrate programmable control over siRNA stoichiometry to achieve sustained, simultaneous silencing of up to four genes from a single entity. Nanostructure assembly alone drives productive delivery, especially to heart and muscle, matching lipophilic conjugation. Furthermore, cerebrospinal fluid administration reveals that larger FMRNs improve central nervous system distribution and retention revealing physicochemical parameters that impact brain exposure. FMRNs establish a modular and effective platform combining improved pharmacokinetics, extrahepatic delivery, and multi-gene silencing for complex diseases.

abstract: Postmenopausal osteoporosis (PO) is not merely a consequence of increased osteoclast activity. Estrogen deficiency induces oxidative stress and pro-inflammatory M1 macrophage polarization in bone tissue, thereby sustaining osteoclastogenic stimuli and pathological bone resorption. Interferon regulatory factor 5 (IRF5) is a key regulator of M1 polarization, and silencing its gene by small interfering RNA (siIRF5) may attenuate the pathogenesis of PO. However, selective delivery of siIRF5 to M1 macrophages within the osteoporotic bone microenvironment is challenging. Herein, we develop a nanomedicine, termed siP@WM, for programmed sequential targeting of bone tissue and macrophages. The siP@WM integrates a platinum nanozyme core with mesoporous silica shell loading siIRF5. The shell with enlarged pores (10-15 nm) provides effective siRNA encapsulation and programmable surface grafting of two kinds of poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) derivatives. The longer poly(aspartic acid)-terminated PEG chain promotes bone enrichment. ROS-triggered thioketal cleavage shortens this chain, reduces bone-matrix adhesion, and exposes the shorter folic acid-functionalized PEG chain to enhance M1 macrophage uptake. In vitro, siP@WM scavenges ROS, facilitates endosomal escape, achieves approximately 60% IRF5 knockdown, and promotes M2 polarization. In ovariectomized mice, systemic administration of siP@WM ameliorates bone loss, restores trabecular microarchitecture and mechanical strength, and shows no overt short-term toxicity in major organs. Transcriptomic and histological analyses support attenuated AP-1-associated inflammatory signaling, suppressed osteoclast differentiation, and modulated extracellular matrix remodeling. Together, programmed siIRF5 delivery to macrophages in bone tissue combined with ROS scavenging restores bone homeostasis and provides an adaptive biomaterial strategy for PO treatment.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Progression of prostate cancer under androgen receptor (AR) pathway-targeted therapy spans a phenotypic spectrum, from tumors that sustain AR pathway output to tumors that become independent of AR signaling. Experimental models that occupy the intermediate portion of this spectrum, in which AR is still expressed but pathway output is reduced, are comparatively scarce.
METHODS: LNCaP cells expressing a triple-modality reporter (LNCaP-TR) were injected into nude mice by the intracardiac route, and a bone lesion that arose in the middle spine of one animal was recovered and propagated as LNCaP-TR-BoM. The subline and its parental line were compared by two-dimensional and three-dimensional culture assays, RNA-seq, qRT-PCR, and immunoblotting. AR pathway output was assessed using KLK3 expression under AR antagonist treatment. Public prostate cancer datasets provided clinical context. A CRISPR-Cas9 EPHA3 -edited derivative was evaluated in aggregation and spheroid assays.
RESULTS: Relative to parental LNCaP-TR, LNCaP-TR-BoM formed more numerous and larger cell aggregates in monolayer culture and larger, less circular spheroids in both suspension and Matrigel three-dimensional culture. AR mRNA was modestly reduced and AR protein remained readily detectable, whereas KLK3 mRNA and protein were reduced disproportionately more than those of AR. Residual KLK3 expression remained suppressible by AR inhibitors enzalutamide and darolutamide. Transcriptome-based pseudotime placed LNCaP-TR-BoM between the parental line and the androgen-refractory LNCaP-RF variant. Subsequent differential gene expression (DGE) and pathway enrichment analysis revealed that LNCaP-TR-BoM exhibits transcriptomic rewiring concordant with that of clinical mCRPC, thus evidencing LNCaP-TR-BoM as a potentially clinically relevant model cell line. Finally, EPHA3 showed the largest fold change among the most significant differentially expressed genes in LNCaP-TR-BoM compared with the parental line. Therefore, EPHA3 was explored to demonstrate the utility of the LNCaP-TR-BoM cell line as a discovery system for genes that potentially drive the malignancy of bone-metastatic prostate cancer at the intermediate AR-attenuated progression stage. An EPHA3 -silenced derivative of LNCaP-TR-BoM lacking detectable EPHA3 protein formed smaller aggregates and smaller, more circular spheroids, suggesting EPHA3 may play a role in driving the malignancy of AR-intermediate bone-metastatic prostate cancer. This finding provides support for the potential utility of the LNCaP-TR-BoM cell line as a discovery system for genes relevant to driving AR-intermediate bone-metastatic prostate cancer.
CONCLUSIONS: LNCaP-TR-BoM is a bone lesion-derived prostate cancer cell line in which AR expression is retained but AR pathway output is attenuated, accompanied by an mCRPC-concordant transcriptomic shift and altered multicellular organization. It provides a paired discovery system for candidate genes such as EPHA3 .

abstract: The self-splicing group I intron ribozyme from Tetrahymena thermophillia (THr) is a prototypical example of how RNA overcomes its limited chemical repertoire to form complex, negatively charged junctions and catalyze chemical reactions. Despite over 30 years of bio-chemical and structural characterization, questions still remain regarding the requirements for THr catalysis that may inform structure based drug design against group I introns, as well as the use of THr as an RNA editing tool. Recent cryo-EM structures have provided an unprecedented window into the first and second steps of splicing, enabling detailed mechanistic investigation at the atomistic level. In this work, we leverage solvation theory, molecular dynamics, alchemical free energy simulations, and machine learning accelerated QM/MM to probe outstanding questions related to 1) the role of a possible third Mg 2+ binding in the active site, 2) differences in catalytic requirements between G exo cofactors and between the first and second steps of splicing, 3) the potential role of an acid or base, and 4) restrictions on the identity of the 5 ' exon splice site nucleotide, U(-1). We propose that a transient, cofactor dependent, interaction with a third metal participates in the first step, while a higher affinity interaction with this third ion is required in the second step. We also propose that the presence of a phosphate on the G exo in the first step, and analogously the G ω in the second step, forms a metal ion binding site not present when guanosine is bound. Finally, we propose and computationally test design modifications of G22 (isofunctional substitutions of 2,6-diaminopurine that tune the p K a at the N1 position) that we predict will enable the accommodation of C(-1) in a crucial wobble-like pair at physiological pH. This design would provide a potential strategy for expanding the sequence space accessible to programmable trans-splicing ribozymes in RNA editing applications.

abstract: Trypanosomatids are medically important single-celled eukaryotic protists with exceptional RNA biology. They display highly unusual RNA biogenesis pathways, notably mitochondrial RNA editing, an essential post-transcriptional process transforming cryptic primary transcripts into functional mRNAs. Large multiprotein assemblies coordinate the RNA editing process, in which small guide RNAs (gRNAs) anneal to the pre-mRNAs and serve as templates for uridine insertion or deletion. Kinetoplast RNA Editing Helicases (KREHs) are important components of the RNA editing process that modifies large portions of pre-mRNA via the sequential annealing and dissociation of multiple gRNAs. However, how KREH helicases interact with components of the editing machinery, and which subunits mediate these interactions, remain unresolved. Here, we examined an association between the DEAH/RHA RNA helicase KREH2 and the RESC1-RESC2 protein heterodimer using proximity labeling and co-immunoprecipitation coupled to quantitative mass spectrometry in vivo . We reconstituted a minimal trimeric KREH2 peptide-RESC1-RESC2 complex in vitro and characterized novel direct binding of a KREH2 peptide to RESC1 using cryo-electron microscopy. These results establish a mechanistic link between the RNA helicase KREH2 and the RESC1-RESC2 module at the 5'-end of gRNAs, providing new avenues for studying the orchestration of RNA remodeling in trypanosomatid mitochondrial RNA editing.

abstract: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) base editors (mtBEs) are promising tools for studying and correcting pathogenic mtDNA mutations. However, the application of mtBEs is often hindered by substantial mtDNA-wide off-target editing that accumulates with prolonged mtBE expression resulting from plasmid DNA or viral delivery. To overcome this limitation, we developed mtBE-VLPs, a virus-like-particle (VLP) platform for transiently delivering mtBEs in vitro and in vivo with minimal off-target effects. While canonical protein-packaging VLPs yielded undetectable mtDNA base editing, engineered mRNA-packaging VLPs enabled efficient but transient mtBE cargo delivery. By iteratively engineering mRNA-packaging VLP compositions, we improved mtBE-VLP-mediated base editing efficiencies from less than 1% to greater than 50% across multiple target mtDNA loci in bulk populations of treated cultured cells. To further improve the packaging and delivery of certain mtBEs, we developed a strategy to selectively reduce mtBE cargo expression in VLP producer cells but not transduced cells, which increased VLP-mediated base editing efficiencies for certain mtBEs by 7.1-fold. Compared to plasmid DNA delivery in vitro , mtBE-VLPs exhibited equivalent on-target editing but 23- to 41-fold lower mtDNA-wide off-target editing, highlighting the improved editing specificity offered by transient mtBE delivery. mtBE-VLPs efficiently installed a pathogenic mtDNA mutation in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (88% efficiency) and corrected a pathogenic mtDNA mutation in a human patient-derived cell line (41% efficiency). Additionally, a single subretinal injection of mtBE-VLPs yielded 6-20% (average 12%) mtDNA base editing in the mouse retinal pigment epithelium with minimal mtDNA-wide off-target editing. These findings establish mRNA-packaging mtBE-VLPs as promising vehicles for efficient and precise mitochondrial base editing via transient mtBE delivery.

abstract:
UNLABELLED: Aberrant monocyte/macrophage activation in diabetes drives chronic inflammation and diabetic complications. Although epigenetic mechanisms are implicated in these processes, the contribution of three-dimensional (3D) chromatin reorganization remains unclear. Here, we use integrated multi-omics approaches to profile gene expression, chromatin accessibility and 3D chromatin architecture in human CD14⁺ monocyte-derived macrophages exposed to high glucose and TNF-α (HT), mimicking the diabetic milieu. HT induces inflammatory transcription programs that recapitulate those observed in diabetes and dynamically remodel chromatin accessibility, enhancer-promoter interactions, and topologically associated domains. Inflammatory genes exhibit increased chromatin accessibility, whereas cell cycle and metabolic genes display reduced accessibility and weakened enhancer-promoter interactions. These architectural changes promote the convergence of lineage-determining and signal-dependent transcription factors at enhancer-promoter loops, generating distinct regulatory hubs that orchestrate pro-inflammatory responses. Similar enhancer-promoter interactions are observed in peripheral blood derived monocytes from individuals with diabetes. Furthermore, perturbing chromatin interactions via CRISPR interference targeting HT-induced enhancers suppresses nearby CCL2 and other chemokine genes. Collectively, this first comprehensive enhancer connectome map of macrophages under diabetic conditions advances the field by revealing extensive disease-associated rewiring of the 3D epigenome, highlighting chromatin architecture and epigenetic mechanisms as potential therapeutic target for diabetes-associated inflammation.
GRAPHICAL ABSTRACT: In diabetes, high glucose (Glc) and inflammatory cytokines remodel macrophage 3D chromatin architecture and enhancer connectomes, altering enhancer-promoter interactions, facilitating the convergence of lineage-specific and signal-dependent transcription factors (such as NF-κB) that regulate inflammatory factors associated with macrophage activation. This can promote chronic inflammation and accelerate diabetic complications. Targeted enhancer editing strategies could enable new epigenetic therapies to mitigate chronic inflammatory diabetes complications.

abstract:
UNLABELLED: Impaired fracture healing remains a significant clinical challenge. Bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) and the exosomes (BMSC-Exos) play a pivotal role in bone regeneration, partly by transferring functional microRNAs (miRNAs). A-to-I RNA editing can profoundly alter miRNA function, but its role in fracture healing, particularly for miRNA-99a-5p, is underexplored. We first profiled differentially edited miRNAs in serum from 50 fracture patients and healthy controls. A murine fracture model was established and treated with BMSC-Exos, where either the edited or wild-type form of miRNA-99a-5p was knocked down. In vitro studies involved transfecting BMSCs with ADAR expression vectors to investigate editing mechanisms, and overexpressing/inhibiting edited/wild-type miRNA-99a-5p in MC3T3-E1C osteoblasts to elucidate its direct functional impacts on osteogenic differentiation, apoptosis, proliferation, and migration. Validation of target genes were performed by dual-luciferase reporter assays, qPCR, and Western blot. Key readouts included alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity, Alizarin Red S (ARS) staining, flow cytometry, Transwell migration, CCK-8 proliferation assays and HE staining. Clinical analysis revealed significantly lower A-to-I edited miRNA-99a-5p levels in fracture patients, correlating with delayed union. In mice, BMSC-Exos promoted fracture healing, an effect attenuated by edited miRNA-99a-5p knockdown. In vitro, edited miRNA-99a-5p enhanced osteogenesis and inhibited apoptosis, while the wild-type form had opposing effects. ADAR2 mediated this editing. Edited miRNA-99a-5p directly targeted and suppressed Growth Differentiation Factor 11 (GDF11) expression. Importantly, GDF11 overexpression reversed the pro-osteogenic effects of edited miRNA-99a-5p, in both direct and exosome-mediated contexts. Reduced A-to-I editing of miRNA-99a-5p is associated with impaired fracture healing. BMSC-Exos facilitate bone repair by delivering ADAR2-edited miRNA-99a-5p, which promotes osteogenic differentiation and bone formation through the specific targeting and downregulation of GDF11. This study uncovers a novel exosome-mediated RNA editing pathway critical for fracture healing and highlights edited miRNA-99a-5p and GDF11 as potential therapeutic targets for bone repair.

title: A-to-I edited miRNA-99a-5p in bone marrow mesenchymal stem cell-derived exosomes promotes fracture healing by regulating GDF11.

abstract: On 16 November 2023, the United Kingdom Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency approved Casgevy (exagamglogene autotemcel), the first CRISPR-based gene therapy for a genetic disease, offering patients with transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia (TDT) freedom from lifelong monthly transfusions. Yet in China, which carries the world's largest TDT patient population, no patient has received the therapy through the public health system, and the access gap is not explained by price or manufacturing economics alone. This paper argues that prevention-era institutional architecture constrains cure-era access through three lock-in mechanisms: cognitive (the direction of genetic information flow), infrastructural (the spatial distribution of treatment capacity), and fiscal (the structure of payment responsibility). Drawing on a structured comparison of four countries selected to represent distinct institutional pathway types (Cyprus, ecclesiastical-public certification; China, administrative filing; Thailand, public health universal coverage; India, federal fragmentation), the analysis proposes a typology of barrier configurations and illustrates them through four exploratory cases. The administrative-filing pathway is associated with high barriers across information, geographic, and economic dimensions; trust-intention is not assessable on current evidence. The ecclesiastical-public pathway is associated with medium information and low geographic barriers with medium fiscal and low-confidence trust barriers; the universal-coverage pathway provides a balanced platform that remains under-activated for gene therapy; and the federal-fragmented pathway fails the precondition of patient identification. No pathway simultaneously optimizes all four readiness dimensions. Presented as a hypothesis-generating typology rather than a tested diagnostic model, the framework relates pathway type to barrier configuration and offers testable hypotheses for pathway-specific intervention design and for extension to sickle cell disease, hemophilia, and other genetic conditions entering the curative era.

title: When prevention constrains cure: Institutional lock-in and gene therapy access for beta-thalassemia.

abstract: Precise, reversible control of transgene expression is essential for safe and durable gene therapy, yet current inducible systems remain difficult to translate in vivo due to large size, limited induction duration, and dependence on immunogenic regulators. Here, we present the adaptamer (adenosine deaminases acting on RNA [ADAR]-modulatable aptamer), a compact (<120 base pair) RNA switch that couples FDA-approved small-molecule-responsive aptamers with endogenous ADAR-mediated RNA editing to regulate expression. Ligand binding stabilizes a double-stranded RNA structure that recruits ADAR to convert a stop codon into a sense codon, restoring downstream protein translation. This cleavage-free, post-transcriptional mechanism enables precise, small-molecule-dependent modulation without exogenous protein machinery. We demonstrate that adaptamers are highly functional across multiple cell lines, including human T cells. In mice, adeno-associated virus (AAV)-delivered adaptamer-controlled FGF21 expression induced metabolic remodeling, reversing obesity and hepatic steatosis. This minimal, programmable system offers a clinically compatible approach for tunable genetic medicines and safe deployment of pleiotropic and dose-limited proteins.

title: Regulatable in vivo gene expression via adaptamers.

abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a prevalent disorder characterized by excessive hepatic lipid accumulation, frequently progressing to steatohepatitis, fibrosis, and cirrhosis. Transcription factor EB (TFEB) coordinates lysosomal biogenesis, autophagy, and lipid catabolism, and therefore represents a potential therapeutic target; however, safe and direct strategies for selectively enhancing hepatic TFEB activity remain limited. Here, liver-targeted lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) were developed to deliver mRNAs encoding wild-type TFEB or the constitutively active TFEB S211A mutant, and their efficacy was evaluated in cellular and choline-deficient, L-amino acid-defined high-fat diet (CDAHFD)-induced mouse models of MASLD. LNP-mediated delivery increased hepatic TFEB expression, enhanced autophagic flux, and reprogrammed metabolic pathways toward fatty acid oxidation (e.g., CPT1A and ACOX1) while suppressing the expression of lipogenic genes (e.g., FASN, ACC, and SREBP1). Consequently, targeted TFEB mRNA therapy significantly reduced hepatic triglyceride content, attenuated steatosis, lowered MASLD activity scores, and decreased fibrotic remodeling. Mechanistically, transcriptomic profiling, ChIP-qPCR, promoter-reporter assays, and targeted knockdown models indicated that TFEB exerts its protective effects against lipid accumulation at least partly by transcriptionally activating the fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) signaling pathway. Collectively, these findings establish LNP-mediated TFEB mRNA delivery as a useful preclinical approach for investigating hepatic biology and provide a targeted, transient, and non-integrating genetic strategy with potential for the treatment of MASLD.

abstract: Background: Parkinson's disease is defined by progressive dopaminergic neurodegeneration and -synuclein pathology. Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and clathrin-mediated endocytosis dysfunction are implicated in disease pathogenesis, but the molecular mechanisms connecting these processes remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate a miR-103a-3p/AGFG1 axis as a regulator link between endocytic trafficking and ER stress in Parkinson's disease. Methods: MiR-103a-3p and AGFG1 were examined in plasma and postmortem substantia nigra from patients with Parkinson's disease and controls. Gain- and loss-of-function studies, target validation and live-cell imaging were used to define the role of the miR-103a-3p/AGFG1 axis in ER stress and endocytic trafficking. The pathway was further investigated in SNCA A53T and LRRK2 G2019S hiPSC-derived neurons. Therapeutic targeting of AGFG1 was evaluated using antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) in vitro and in a 6-hydroxydopamine mouse model. Results: MiR-103a-3p was significantly reduced in Parkinson's disease plasma and substantia nigra, whereas AGFG1 was increased in nigral tissue. MiR-103a-3p directly repressed AGFG1 and attenuated thapsigargin-induced ER stress, while miR-103a-3p inhibition or AGFG1 overexpression exacerbated stress signalling. AGFG1 knockdown reversed the effects of miR-103a-3p inhibition, establishing AGFG1 as a functional downstream effector. Mechanistically, AGFG1 associated and co-trafficked with clathrin-positive vesicles, whereas ER stress progressively disrupted AGFG1-clathrin vesicle dynamics, revealing an association between endocytic trafficking and stress signalling. In genetic Parkinson's disease models, SNCA A53T and LRRK2 G2019S neurons showed mutation-dependent differences in AGFG1 expression and stress regulation. eIF2 phosphorylation increased in both SNCA A53T and LRRK2 G2019S neurons, whereas AGFG1 and GADD34 upregulation was selective to SNCA A53T neurons. Importantly, ASO-mediated AGFG1 suppression attenuated ER stress in vitro and preserved nigral dopaminergic neurons with improved motor performance in vivo. Conclusion: Our findings identify the miR-103a-3p/AGFG1 axis as a previously unrecognised molecular link between endocytic trafficking dysfunction and ER stress in Parkinson's disease, and support AGFG1 as a mechanistically potential therapeutic target.

abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-engineered natural killer (NK) cell therapy has emerged as a promising immunotherapeutic strategy for cancer treatment, offering advantages over CAR-T cells such as a lower risk of cytokine release syndrome and graft-versus-host disease and the potential for off-the-shelf manufacturing. Viral vectors have long served as effective tools for CAR-NK engineering, but their dependence on complex manufacturing procedures, considerable production costs, and the potential risks associated with genomic integration has encouraged increasing interest in non-viral alternatives. Recent advances in genetic engineering technologies have facilitated the development of CAR-NK platforms, particularly through non-viral delivery approaches including electroporation, transposon systems and lipid nanoparticles, while CRISPR-based tools enable targeted genome editing. Meanwhile, an increasing number of clinical trials have begun to evaluate the safety and therapeutic potential of CAR-NK cells in both hematological malignancies and solid tumors. However, challenges such as limited NK-cell persistence, antigen heterogeneity, and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment remain. In this review, we summarize recent progress in non-viral CAR-NK engineering strategies, analyze the current landscape of preclinical and clinical trials, and discuss key challenges and future directions for advancing CAR-NK therapy. Collectively, these advances suggest that non-viral engineering technologies may serve as an important technological foundation for next-generation CAR-NK therapies, enabling more flexible ex vivo manufacturing and potentially supporting the future development of in vivo CAR-NK generation strategies for solid tumors.

abstract: Colorectal cancer liver metastasis (CRLM) remains a major cause of cancer mortality, yet the metabolic mechanisms that remodel metastatic RNA-splicing programs are poorly defined. Here, integrated quantitative proteomics and lysine 2-hydroxyisobutyrylation (Khib) proteomics of patient-matched normal mucosa, primary CRCs, and liver metastases revealed a progressive increase in global Khib, with enrichment on RNA-splicing proteins. Serine/arginine-rich splicing factor 9 (SRSF9) emerged as a Khib-modified splicing factor whose expression and K155 Khib levels increased from normal tissue to primary tumors and liver metastases. Gain and loss of function studies in CRC cell lines, patient-derived organoids, subcutaneous xenografts, and splenic injection liver metastasis models showed that SRSF9 promotes proliferation, invasion, tumor growth, and liver colonization. Mechanistically, K155 Khib stabilized SRSF9 protein; the K155R mutation accelerated degradation and abolished SRSF9-driven malignant phenotypes. KAT7 and SIRT6 act as regulators of Khib modification, which positively and negatively modulate the K155 Khib modification of SRSF9, respectively. SRSF9 bound CD44 pre-mRNA through its RRM1 domain and promoted alternative splicing toward the oncogenic CD44V8-10 isoform, which was elevated in patient tumors and metastases and rescued the impaired proliferation and metastatic capacity caused by SRSF9 loss. Finally, a CD44V8-10-targeting antisense oligonucleotide suppressed CRC growth and liver metastasis in preclinical models. These findings define a KAT7/SIRT6-regulated Khib-SRSF9-CD44V8-10 axis that couples metabolic acylation to metastatic splicing and nominate CD44V8-10 as a therapeutic vulnerability in CRC liver metastasis.

abstract: The recent CRISPR-Cas12b gene editing system, which recognizes DNA targets based on reprogrammed RNA, is increasingly being utilized in various fields. We developed an advanced base-editing technology that seamlessly integrates the TadA8e deaminase with an inactivated dBhCas12b (dead Bacillus hisashii Cas12b) module, enabling precise single-base DNA substitutions in human cell lines. Using the TadA8e-dBhCas12b module, we successfully induced single-base (A-to-G) substitutions at genomic target sites in HEK293FT cells, with an efficiency ranging from 3.96% ± 1.10%-25.78% ± 0.78%, with minimal unintended indel formation due to target DNA nicking. Notably, the editing window of the TadA8e-dBhCas12b module, spanning approximately positions 5-10, can be precisely modulated through the introduction of point mutations within the RuvC domain and the fusion of nonspecific DNA-binding domains, such as Sso7d. These modifications enable efficient base editing at target sites containing thymine-rich protospacer-adjacent motifs (PAMs). The optimized TadA8e-dBhCas12b platform therefore represents a complementary alternative to conventional CRISPR-Cas9-derived base editors and may broaden the range of targetable pathogenic variants, particularly those located within T-rich genomic contexts. Its DNA context-dependent editing window and expanded targeting capacity highlight its potential utility in both basic biological research and therapeutic genome editing.

title: Minimal indel-inducing and window-adjustable base editing using inactive Cas12b effectors.

abstract: Spherical nucleic acids (SNAs) are a unique class of nucleic acid nanotherapeutics characterized by densely packed, radially arranged oligonucleotides surrounding a nanoparticle or molecular core, or core-free nanoscale structures. Compared with conventional linear nucleic acids, SNAs exhibit excellent cellular uptake, resistance to nuclease degradation, and efficient target recognition without the help of transfection agents. This review summarizes SNAs' structural diversity, design principles, and the multiscale delivery barriers they encounter. We mainly focus on liposomal SNAs (LSNAs) as programmable platforms for cancer immunotherapy. We emphasize how lipid chemistry, membrane architecture, and anchor stability control lymphoid distribution, immune-cell uptake, antigen presentation, and strong antitumor immunity, rather than seeing lipids as inert carriers. Furthermore, we also discuss current developments in gene silencing, CRISPR-based genome editing, and stimulus-responsive multimodal therapies, highlighting the significant therapeutic advancements of SNAs like clinical trial NU-0129 and LSNAs like cavrotolimod. Finally, we describe present translational obstacles and potential prospects by using SNAs as next-generation precision immunotherapeutics.

abstract: Sepsis-associated encephalopathy (SAE) represents the most prevalent neurological complication arising from sepsis, affecting approximately 70% of patients with sepsis and associated with mortality rates reaching up to 70%. Survivors frequently experience persistent cognitive deficits; however, the field currently lacks specific diagnostic biomarkers and targeted therapeutic interventions, with diagnosis primarily established through exclusion criteria. This review critically examines multi-omic investigations of SAE, evaluating whether convergent evidence across genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic domains elucidates shared pathophysiological mechanisms and identifying prevailing translational challenges. The synthesis of evidence is structured around three interrelated thematic domains. First, multi-omic analyses have elucidated the initial triggers of neuroinflammation: genomic studies implicate Piezo1-mediated oligodendrocyte ferroptosis and adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing, while proteomic data corroborate activation of the reactive oxygen species (ROS)/thioredoxin-interacting protein (TXNIP)/NLRP3 inflammasome axis, collectively indicating that peripheral inflammatory cues converge upon central innate immune pathways. Second, transcriptomic and proteomic findings converge on microglial polarization as a pivotal mediator in SAE progression: single-cell sequencing reveals C1q-dependent synaptic pruning, S100A9 protein expression promotes pro-inflammatory microglial polarization, and metabolomic profiles demonstrate that cyclophilin D (CypD)-regulated redox imbalances modulate the magnitude of glial inflammatory responses. Third, integrative analyses delineate neuronal injury pathways: the NAT10 (N-acetyltransferase 10)/GABA(B) receptor 1 axis is implicated in inhibitory synaptic dysfunction through coordinated transcriptomic and proteomic alterations, while elevated levels of 4-hydroxyphenylacetic acid correlate with impaired consciousness, suggesting its potential utility as a prognostic biomarker. Across these domains-initiation, mediation, and injury-multi-omic integration further extends the conceptual framework to encompass systemic regulation via the microbiota-gut-brain axis. Notwithstanding these advances, extant evidence is limited by predominantly cross-sectional study designs, reliance on single-animal models, and a paucity of rigorous clinical validation. To address these limitations, we propose a three-tiered cascade model-comprising Inflammation Initiation, Glial Mediation, and Neuronal Injury-that synthesizes current findings into a coherent, testable framework. Furthermore, we delineate a methodological roadmap emphasizing longitudinal sampling, multi-center validation, causal inference methodologies, and artificial intelligence-driven data integration. This review endeavors not only to consolidate existing knowledge but also to establish an actionable translational paradigm aimed at advancing SAE research from descriptive characterization toward precision diagnostics and mechanism-based therapeutic strategies.

title: Multi-omics advances in sepsis-associated encephalopathy: from pathogenesis to clinical translation.

abstract: Therapeutic mRNA vaccines are a clinically validated cancer immunotherapy platform using in vitro transcribed mRNA encoding tumor antigens to induce durable anti-tumor immunity. Advances in mRNA engineering, lipid nanoparticle (LNP) delivery, and immunomodulatory combinations have propelled this approach from preclinical models to randomized trials with survival benefit. This review systematically examines vaccine efficacy through an antigen-delivery-immunomodulation tripartite framework. We trace the evolution from shared tumor-associated antigens to personalized neoantigens identified by computational pipelines, discuss ionizable lipid chemistry and LNP formulation for controlled tissue tropism and transfection, and analyze the bidirectional crosstalk between vaccine components and innate immune sensing that shapes adaptive T cell responses. Clinical evidence across melanoma, pancreatic cancer, non-small cell lung cancer, and other solid tumors is critically evaluated, alongside combination strategies-checkpoint blockade, oncolytic virotherapy, and adoptive cell therapy to overcome TME resistance. Persistent challenges include optimal neoantigen selection, standardized immune monitoring, and predictive biomarkers. We conclude that future research should prioritize systematic optimization of the tripartite design through multi-antigen targeting, tissue-specific delivery engineering, and rational combination immunotherapy, aiming to establish mRNA cancer vaccines as a standard-of-care modality.

title: Progress on therapeutic mRNA vaccines for cancer.

abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have risen to the forefront of modern therapeutics by enabling the clinical success of COVID-19 mRNA vaccines. In order for them to function as drug delivery vesicles, LNPs must have scalable, tunable, and targeted nanoscale platforms whose strengths in versatility, performance, and clinical relevance are driven by key design parameters and formulation strategies. This Tutorial Review traces the historical evolution of LNPs and examines the fundamental design principles governing their structure, physicochemical properties, and biological behavior. It further highlights modern analytical characterization techniques that have advanced mechanistic understanding of LNP composition, morphology, and function as well as targeting strategies to improve LNP delivery to extrahepatic sites. Current translational challenges and emerging advances are also discussed. This Tutorial Review provides a framework for understanding the foundations, current landscape, and future directions of LNP research.

title: Lipid Nanoparticles at the Crossroads of Chemistry and Medicine: A Tutorial.

abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and osteoarthritis (OA) are debilitating joint disorders with distinct etiologies but share common pathological features of chronic inflammation and progressive cartilage damage. Current therapeutic options are largely palliative and yet fail to achieve desired effect. In this study, we developed a combinatorial mRNA therapy using a rationally engineered lipid nanoparticle (LNP) containing a novel ionizable lipid for enhanced cartilage penetration upon intra-articular administration. This LNP co-delivers mRNAs encoding two complementary therapeutic proteins: interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra) for inflammation attenuation and a C-terminal truncated derivative of angiopoietin-like 3 (ANL3) for cartilage degeneration prevention. In pre-clinical models including collagen-induced arthritis mice, TNF-transgenic mice with spontaneous RA and destabilization of medial meniscus (DMM) surgical OA model, this dual therapy significantly ameliorated disease severity, reduced synovitis and bone erosion, and potently repaired cartilage damage. Mechanistically, transcriptomic profiling of joint specimens revealed that the combinatorial therapy concurrently suppressed inflammatory pathways and extracellular matrix degradation pathways, meanwhile upregulating anabolic genes facilitating chondrogenesis. Collectively, our study establishes a versatile and synergistic mRNA therapy that offers a potent disease-modifying immunomodulatory strategy capable of addressing the long-standing unmet needs in arthritis treatment.

title: A Combinatorial mRNA Therapy for Treating Rheumatoid Arthritis and Osteoarthritis by Inhibiting Inflammation and Preventing Cartilage Degeneration.

abstract: Over the past decade, CRISPR-Cas based biosensors have emerged as sensitive, specific and programmable platforms for nucleic acid detection, with applications ranging from diagnostic tools, environmental monitoring and various applications in fundamental research. The vast majority of these biosensors are currently limited to in vitro applications, highlighting the need for cellular platforms. Here, we provide a perspective on the potential of type III CRISPR-Cas systems as a platform for real-time RNA biosensing in living cells. We discuss the unique properties that distinguish type III from other CRISPR-Cas types, including their intrinsic cyclic oligoadenylate (cOA) signal amplification cascade, PAM-free RNA targeting and the extensive biochemical diversity of their downstream CARF and SAVED effector proteins. We outline the fundamental design principles of a genetically encoded type III cellular biosensor, comprising a programmable guide RNA, a multi-subunit sensing complex and a cOA-sensing effector protein capable of generating optical or electrochemical readout signals. A remaining challenge for type III cellular biosensors is the inherent cytotoxicity of canonical cOA-activated effectors. We propose several strategies to re-engineer these outputs towards non-cytotoxic reporter systems. While cellular biosensors present a natural route toward in vivo sensing, they face many challenges beyond the choice of the output signal and hardware strategy. We conclude that type III CRISPR-Cas is a promising platform for programmable real-time RNA sensing in living cells, utilizing its diverse modular effector outputs, representing a significant expansion of the CRISPR biosensor toolkit, while emphasizing appropriate deployment scenarios that enables full potential of these biosensors.

title: Repurposing Type III CRISPR-Cas as Modular Cellular RNA Biosensors.

abstract: MYC is among the most frequently amplified oncogenes in human cancer, yet its intrinsically disordered nature has rendered it refractory to direct pharmacological targeting. Here, we demonstrate that the long noncoding RNA NEAT1_1 functions as a molecular gatekeeper that controls MYC protein stability by regulating its access to the E3 ubiquitin ligase UBR5. We show that NEAT1_1 forms a ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complex with both MYC and UBR5, and that NEAT1_1 suppression disrupts this interaction, leading to decreased MYC polyubiquitination and enhanced protein stability. To systematically map the regulatory architecture of NEAT1_1 without altering its abundance, we screened 88 antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) mixmers tiling across the transcript. Strikingly, this phenotypic screen identified region-specific mixmers that elicit bidirectional control over MYC, either driving robust MYC destabilization or promoting its stabilization in a strictly expression-independent manner. Mechanistically, MYC-destabilizing mixmers selectively enhance the interaction between MYC and UBR5 to accelerate proteasomal degradation. A focused CRISPR screen targeting the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway independently validated UBR5 as the essential E3 ligase mediating this mixmer-induced turnover. In vivo, our lead mixmer ASO_#24 significantly suppressed tumor growth in MYC-high xenografts, whereas MYC-low tumors remained unaffected. Our findings reveal that the functional output of a scaffold lncRNA is encoded in its sub-domain architecture rather than bulk transcript levels, establishing domain-specific RNA targeting as a tractable strategy to rewire protein turnover pathways for otherwise undruggable oncogenes.

title: NEAT1 remodeling rewires the MYC degradation pathway.

abstract: RNA 5-methylcytidine (m5C) modification plays an essential role in regulating RNA metabolism and functions in cellular processes. Tools to achieve temporal and transcript-specific m5C editing for functional studies are still limited. Furthermore, methods enabling m5C editing triggered by specific cellular signals to study m5C functions are currently lacking. Here, we present a temporally and conditionally controlled m5C writing platform engineered through integrating abscisic acid (ABA)-mediated chemically induced proximity with split-dCas13b-NSUN2/NSUN6 technology. This system enables the writing of m5C by reconstituting the split dCas13b-based m5C editing complex at the guide RNA (gRNA)-targeted RNA transcript sites under the control of the inducer ABA. The deposition of m5C is inducible, reversible and selective. The deposited m5C is biologically active and influences the stability of endogenous mRNA transcripts. Moreover, by incorporating ABA prodrugs, the m5C writing can be triggered by signals associated with distinct physiological or disease conditions (e.g., tumor microenvironment and senescence). This conditional m5C editing strategy provides a new programmable tool for studying m5C biology in a context-dependent manner and expands the repertoire of RNA modification editing technologies.

title: Cellular signal-responsive m5C editing by an inducible split CRISPR platform.

abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is driven by cancer stemness and an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, which collectively contribute to therapeutic resistance. While the RNA-binding protein HNRNPC has been implicated in tumor progression, it has primarily been characterized as a downstream effector, and its autonomous regulatory functions, particularly in governing cancer stemness, remain entirely unexplored. Through multi-omics analyses of HCC cohorts, we identified HNRNPC as a pivotal driver of a high-risk molecular subtype. Mechanistically, HNRNPC expression was transcriptionally activated via WDR5/KMT2A complex-mediated deposition of H3K4me3 at its promoter. Functionally, HNRNPC was essential for maintaining cancer stemness, promoting tumor growth and metastasis, and conferring oxaliplatin resistance. Notably, depletion of HNRNPC reprogrammed the immunosuppressive microenvironment by enhancing CD8+ T cell infiltration, reducing T cell exhaustion, and polarizing macrophages toward an M1-like anti-tumor phenotype. At the molecular level, HNRNPC bound to the m6A-modified 3'UTR of CD24 mRNA in an RNP2 motif-dependent manner, thereby enhancing its stability and elevating CD24 protein expression. Therapeutically, we developed a novel lipid nanoparticle (LNP) encapsulating siRNA against HNRNPC. Systemically administered AP-EG-si potently suppressed tumor growth, attenuated stemness, and synergized with anti-PD-L1 therapy to enhance anti-tumor immunity. Our findings thus unveil the H3K4me3-HNRNPC-CD24 axis as a central epigenetic and post-transcriptional regulatory pathway that coordinately drives HCC stemness and immune evasion, nominating HNRNPC-targeted nanotherapy as a promising strategy for advanced HCC.

title: Targeting the H3K4me3-HNRNPC-CD24 Axis Overcomes Stemness and Immunosuppression in Hepatocellular Carcinoma.

abstract: This protocol describes a method for endogenous protein tagging in postmitotic primary neurons using homology-independent targeted integration (HITI), a CRISPR/Cas9-based approach that exploits non-homologous end joining (NHEJ). Unlike homology-directed repair (HDR), HITI does not require cell division, making it uniquely suited for postmitotic neurons. SpCas9 is delivered by a replication-incompetent simian immunodeficiency lentiviral vector (pLenti SIV), while the sgRNA, donor tag cassette, and a fluorescent plasma membrane marker are co-packaged in a single AAV vector. The two vectors are co-delivered at DIV5, and endogenous tagging is assessed at DIV15-23. The workflow is illustrated using Junctophilin-3 (JPH3) tagged with mEmerald at its endogenous locus. Airyscan microscopy imaging of endogenously tagged JPH3 at native expression levels revealed its localization at endoplasmic reticulum-plasma membrane (ER-PM) contact sites and uncovered a periodic distribution of ER-PM junctions along the dendritic arbor, enabling identification of a previously unrecognized ladder-like organization of the ER in neuronal dendrites. Genomic integration of the tag is validated at both 5' and 3' junctions by next-generation sequencing. The protocol can be adapted to other neuronal proteins by redesigning the guide RNA and donor sequence, and supports fluorescent proteins as well as epitope and self-labeling tags. The plasma membrane marker can also be replaced with other fluorescent reporters or markers for intracellular organelles to assess infection efficiency and verify subcellular localization of the protein of interest. The full workflow takes 5-6 weeks. © 2026 The Author(s). Current Protocols published by Wiley Periodicals LLC. Protocols included in this article: Basic Protocol 1: sgRNA design and HITI donor vector cloning Basic Protocol 2: Primary rat neuron culture and viral co-transduction Basic Protocol 3: Live-cell imaging of endogenously tagged proteins Support Protocol 1: Production of lentiviral and AAV particles Support Protocol 2: Validation of knock-in by next-generation sequencing (NGS).

title: Endogenous Protein Tagging in Postmitotic Neurons via Lentiviral and Adeno-associated Virus Delivery.

abstract: Inherited platelet disorders (IPDs) comprise a heterogeneous group of rare genetic diseases affecting platelet production and/or function, with clinical manifestations ranging from mild mucocutaneous bleeding to severe hemorrhage, multisystem disease, and predisposition to hematologic malignancy. Treatment remains predominantly supportive, and curative options are limited. Future translation will require disease-specific selection of gene addition, allele-specific approaches, or precise genome editing, together with safer conditioning, efficient lineage-restricted correction, and rigorous long-term assessment of genotoxicity and clonal evolution. A shared hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells platform combined with disease-specific genetic engineering may ultimately enable curative treatment of selected severe IPDs.

title: Gene Therapy for Inherited Platelet Disorders: From Proof of Concept to Clinical Translation.

abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has emerged as one of the most severe global health threats. The rapid expansion of multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) pathogens compromises the effectiveness of conventional antibiotics. Globally, ESKAPE organisms (Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Enterobacter spp.) have led to therapeutic failure, prolonged hospitalization, and increased mortality rates. This review identifies the molecular mechanisms, including enzymatic antibiotic inactivation, efflux pump overexpression, biofilm formation, and horizontal gene transfer, that underline the resistance of disseminated pathogens to antibiotics in clinical, agricultural, and environmental settings. Antibiotic overuse and pharmaceutical and agricultural discharges create persistent reservoirs for the dissemination of AMR genes. Furthermore, we evaluated the non-traditional antibacterial efficacy of antimicrobial peptides, bacteriophage therapy, monoclonal antibodies, probiotics, fecal microbiota transplantation, anti-virulence agents, CRISPR-Cas precision antimicrobials, and nanotechnology-based drug delivery platforms. Current preclinical and clinical evidence indicates the eradication of resistant pathogens, disruption of biofilms, and preservation of host microbiota, thereby reducing the selective pressure associated with broad-spectrum antibiotics. Despite these advances, major translational barriers, such as pharmacokinetic instability, manufacturing limitations, and insufficient clinical validation, restrict the implementation of the framework. In the future, the AMR management framework will require precision medicine, artificial intelligence, and One Health-based integration via multidisciplinary collaboration.

title: Combating Antimicrobial Resistance: Emerging Non-Traditional Therapeutics, Clinical Translation Challenges, and Future Perspectives.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Efficient, reproducible gene knockout in cardiomyocyte-related cell models is critical for cardiovascular research but remains challenging because of cell-type-specific sensitivity to genome-editing workflows.
METHODS: We developed an optimized CRISPR-Cas9 genome-editing protocol using electroporation of ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes to generate knockout lines in cardiac and skeletal muscle cells. We also provide practical guidance for gRNA design, genotyping, and clonal line generation. Using human AC16 cardiomyocyte-like cells and rodent muscle-derived cell lines (C2C12, L6, and H9C2), we optimized electroporation conditions to maximize editing efficiency while maintaining viability.
RESULTS: SpCas9-single-guide RNA (sgRNA) RNPs targeting the lipid-trafficking regulator SAR1B/Sar1b produced high-frequency frameshift indels and marked loss of target protein expression in all models. A composite knockout score that combines editing efficiency and cell survival identified optimal electroporation settings of 1400 V, 10 ms, and 3 pulses for AC16 cells, and 1500 V, 10 ms, and 3 pulses for C2C12, L6, and H9C2 cells.
CONCLUSIONS: This protocol combines rational sgRNA design, chemically modified sgRNAs for efficient RNP assembly, and standardized genotyping to improve reproducibility. The framework is transferable to other cardiomyocyte and muscle-derived cell types and supports both pthe olyclonal and monoclonal CRISPR-Cas9 knockout approaches.

title: A DNA-free CRISPR-Cas9 ribonucleoprotein electroporation protocol for efficient knockout generation in cardiac and skeletal muscle cell lines.

abstract: Rapid and accurate diagnostics are essential for controlling emerging infectious diseases and antimicrobial resistance, yet CRISPR assays with exceptional analytical sensitivity often remain difficult to translate into deployable tests. Existing reviews have commonly organized CRISPR diagnostics by Cas effector, biosensor format, or application, offering limited guidance on how design decisions interact across complete workflows or why promising systems remain at the proof-of-concept stage. We introduce an integrated framework that connects five coupled design layers with five levels of translational evidence. The design layers comprise guide RNA engineering, signal amplification circuits, molecular adaptors, computational design support, and specimen and intended-use implementation. The evidence levels progress from purified-target characterization and spiked-matrix testing to retrospective specimen evaluation, prospective integrated-workflow evaluation, and intended-use operation by target users supported by controls, usability assessment, real-time stability, manufacturing consistency, cost per valid result, and claim-specific regulatory preparation. This dual framework shows how improvements at one layer can shift the dominant bottleneck to another. For example, preamplification can lower the analytical limit of detection while increasing contamination risk and workflow burden, whereas guide designs that improve sequence discrimination may reduce cognate-target activation. The framework supports bottleneck-guided selection of effectors, signal-gain strategies, adaptors, computational tools, and multiplexing formats according to target type and abundance, specimen matrix, intended decision, target users, and deployment setting. High analytical sensitivity or single-nucleotide discrimination under controlled conditions does not establish clinical utility unless such performance improves classification at the intended decision threshold within the complete workflow. Translation requires standardized benchmarking, matrix-aware validation, appropriate controls, stability and manufacturability assessment, prospective intended-use studies, and economic evaluation suited to the intended claim and setting. This framework shifts the evaluation of CRISPR diagnostics from isolated analytical performance toward evidence-based workflow co-design.

title: Molecular Programming of CRISPR Diagnostics: From Target Recognition to Field Deployment.

abstract: Given the growing emphasis on the efficient application of CRISPR/Cas9 in plant genome editing, there is a need for methodologies that enhance targeted mutagenesis efficiency. In the present study, we utilized stable transgenic maize callus tissues harboring active CRISPR/Cas9 vector systems targeting either the abnormal cytokinin response 1 (ARE1) gene or the potassium channel gene (KAT2). The presented DNA sequencing data indicate that the KAT2-targeting vector, which utilizes a 3'-end truncated guide RNA, retained mutagenic activity, albeit at a notably low frequency. We quantified mutagenic events following exposure to elevated temperatures (37 °C for 48 h) and various chromatin-modifying compounds, including sodium butyrate (NaBt), nicotinamide (NA), and 5-azacytidine (AZA). High-temperature treatment alone increased the frequency of nucleotide deletions (5.8-fold relative to the untreated samples) in the ARE1 target gene. Conversely, in the KAT2 gene, both deletions and insertions were stimulated (6.4 and 6.2-fold, respectively). As a novel approach, we evaluated the mutagenic efficacy of chromatin-modifying compounds administered in conjunction with heat treatment. The combined application of NaBt and AZA with elevated temperature was particularly effective in increasing insertion frequencies; in the ARE1 (with NaBt + heat: 17.3-fold) and KAT2 (with AZA + heat: 21.4-fold) genes. Cell cycle analysis of suspension-cultured cells revealed that chromatin-modifying treatments altered cell cycle progression, evidenced by an accumulation of cells in the G2 phase and a significant reduction in the number of mitotic cells. Subsequent DNA sequencing demonstrated a differential increase in the induction of deletions and insertions, alongside an expansion of the deleted regions.

title: Variable alterations in frequencies of CRISPR/Cas9-induced nucleotide deletion and insertion in transgenic maize callus tissues exposed to chromatin modifiers.

abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a major cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. Emerging evidence has established N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA methylation as a key epitranscriptomic mechanism underlying hepatocarcinogenesis. Methyltransferase-like 3 (METTL3), the catalytic core of the m6A methyltransferase complex (MTC), forms a heterodimer with METTL14 and cooperates with auxiliary components of the MTC to deposit m6A modifications that modulate mRNA stability, splicing, nuclear export, and translation. In this review, we comprehensively summarize the current understanding of METTL3 biology in HCC, focusing on its structure, assembly within the MTC, regulation of coding and non-coding RNAs, and its roles in driving key oncogenic signaling cascades, such as JAK/STAT3, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, Wnt/β-catenin, Hippo/YAP, Notch, Hedgehog, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. In addition, we discussed how METTL3 remodels the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) by regulating immune responses and metabolic pathways promoting immune evasion and therapy resistance. Therapeutic strategies targeting METTL3-including small-molecule inhibitors, CRISPR-Cas9 approaches, combination immunotherapy, and tumor-selective delivery systems-are discussed together with the challenges that continue to limit clinical translation. Collectively, these findings position METTL3 as a central epitranscriptomic regulator of HCC progression; however, further mechanistic and clinical validation remains necessary to establish its utility as a therapeutic target and prognostic biomarker.

abstract: Antisense oligonucleotides (ASO) are nucleotide polymers that hybridize to sense strands and have been successful in treating a variety of diseases. A wide range of strategies have been investigated to optimize and develop ASO for clinical studies. A key objective for this study was to provide an overview of the range of detailed data that can be obtained and provide an updated method review on how to design surface plasmon resonance (SPR) kinetic experiments for DNA oligonucleotide hybridization studies that can also be applied to other ASO including peptide nucleic acids (PNA). We describe many lessons learned from published literature and provide a state-of-the-art strategy and methods for generating not only kinetic but also thermodynamic characterizations of oligonucleotide hybridization. In this study we have performed an SPR kinetic and thermodynamic analysis for the hybridization of HIF1 antisense DNA strands to its immobilized Intron2-Exon3 splice site sense DNA strand to provide insight, in general, on the optimal length and insight into optimal design of DNA ASOs. We provide a process on how to design experiments to: 1.) obtain oligonucleotide-length dependent kinetics, 2.) analyze reactions to obtain association and dissociation rate kinetics (ka, kd), assess if hybridization follows a 2-state model and to obtain kinetic dissociation constants (Kd), 3.) perform temperature-dependent hybridization kinetics to obtain thermodynamic values ({Delta}H{degrees}, {Delta}S{degrees} and {Delta}G{degrees}) that can give insight into the molecular interactions driving hybridization, 4.) compare experimental thermodynamic values to values derived from nearest-neighbor prediction models to identify atypical reactions and importantly 5.) enable calculations to predict oligomer hybridization affinity at the physiological 37 {degrees}C temperature to assess if the design of the oligomer will have the required cellular activity for a therapeutic effect. The strategy and results presented throughout the paper are compared to previous SPR reports and suggestions made to optimize kinetic studies.

abstract:
BACKGROUND/PURPOSE: We have shown that extracellular vesicles (EVs) derived from Polygonum multiflorum extract bio-pulsed avian mesenchymal stem cells exhibit anti-inflammatory and proliferation-promoting properties. A significant association has been identified between periodontitis, higher biological age, and accelerated biological aging. This study investigated whether the bio-pulsed EVs could alleviate Porphyromonas gingivalis lipopolysaccharide (Pg-LPS)-induced senescence in human gingival fibroblasts (hGFs).
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Pg-LPS was used to induce cellular inflammation and senescence in hGFs. The cytokines IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α were assessed by quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR), and cytotoxicity was assessed with MTS. Senescence after repeated stimulations was evaluated by flow cytometry, SA-β-gal staining, and p16, p21, and p53 mRNA and protein (qPCR and Western blot), and telomere length (qPCR). Cell proliferation and apoptosis markers of Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) were evaluated by colorimetric assay.
RESULTS: Cytotoxicity was noted in hGFs only at 5.0 μg/mL LPS. LPS at 0.5 μg/mL significantly upregulated IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α mRNA expressions. Repeated LPS significantly increased cell size (1.0 μg/mL), the number of SA-β-gal-staining cells (0.5 and 1.0 μg/mL), and mRNA and protein expressions for p16, p21, and p53 (1.0 μg/mL), indicating senescence. Bio-pulsed EVs significantly increased CCK-8 but reduced LDH releases, indicating improved hGFs viability. Furthermore, the bio-pulsed EVs suppressed the LPS-induced upregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines and senescence markers, but reversed telomere shortening.
CONCLUSION: Single Pg LPS triggered inflammatory responses in hGFs, whereas repeated exposures induced senescence. The bio-pulsed EVs effectively mitigated Pg LPS-induced inflammation and senescence, highlighting the preventive/therapeutic potential.

abstract: Brassicaceae crops are globally important economic plants, whose yield and quality directly affect the supply of edible oil and vegetables. Most of these crops are polyploids with complex genomes and numerous homoeologous gene copies, which demand high efficiency and specificity from gene editing tools, while providing ideal models for studying the rules of polyploid genome editing. Traditional breeding methods, such as crossbreeding and mutation breeding, are constrained by long cycles, low efficiency, and poor specificity, making them insufficient for precise genetic improvement. Gene editing technologies, characterized by precision, efficiency, and targeting specific genomic loci, are core tools for crop breeding. Among these, ZFNs and TALENs rely on protein-DNA recognition and are complicated and costly to design; CRISPR-Cas, which achieves precise recognition through base pairing between guide RNA and target DNA, is simple, efficient, and the most widely used editing tool. Base and prime editors enable single-nucleotide substitutions or small fragment insertions without generating double-strand breaks, making them suitable for directed modification of point mutations. This review summarizes the progress of gene editing in Brassicaceae for bolting/flowering, plant architecture, nutritional quality, tolerance to abiotic stresses (temperature, salinity, drought, heavy metals), and resistance to biotic stresses (diseases, pests). We analyze challenges, including off-target effects, difficulties in polyploid genome editing, and imperfect genetic transformation systems, and discuss future directions integrating gene editing with multi-omics and artificial intelligence. This review aims to provide a theoretical basis and technical support for precise molecular breeding of Brassicaceae crops.

title: Research progress in gene editing of Brassicaceae crops.

abstract: Plant base editing enables targeted nucleotide substitutions and provides a powerful approach for functional genomics and crop improvement. The toolkit has expanded from canonical cytosine and adenine editors to dual-base, transversion, Cas12-based, and organelle-targeted systems, broadening the range of accessible mutations and genomic targets. These advances create new opportunities for generating useful alleles, modifying gene function, and enabling directed evolution. However, expanded base-editing capabilities do not necessarily ensure predictable outcomes or successful breeding applications. This review summarizes the development of plant base editors, computational tools for target design, and their applications in crop research. We examine editor architectures and compare editing efficiency, product purity, and specificity, with particular attention to transversion editing. We also highlight the intrinsic technical limitations of base editors and the bottlenecks encountered when moving from laboratory research to field applications. By connecting base editor development with practical constraints, this review provides guidance for editor selection and identifies priorities for applying base editing to crop improvement.

title: From base transitions to expanded editing tools: development and applications of plant base editors.

abstract: Trypanosoma brucei and Leishmania tarentolae are model kinetoplastids whose mitochondria contain a unique DNA network, kinetoplast DNA (kDNA), and exhibit specialized features, including developmental remodeling and RNA editing. By integrating mass spectrometry-based protein correlation profiling with published datasets, we assembled inventories of 1,666 mitochondrial proteins in T. brucei and 1,594 in L. tarentolae. These include 124 polypeptides not previously recognized as mitochondrial. Despite their phylogenetic distance, trypanosomes and leishmanias maintain highly conserved mitoproteomes, including about 700 components with no detectable homologs in other eukaryotes. Comparison of T. brucei insect and mammalian stages revealed similar mitoproteome compositions but globally reduced mitochondrial protein abundance in the latter, except for components of calcium homeostasis and the alternative oxidase pathway. We also detected ten kDNA-encoded proteins, including products of pan-edited transcripts. These inventories establish a framework for functional analysis of previously uncharacterized mitochondrial factors and illuminate innovations that have shaped kinetoplastid evolution.

title: Lineage-specific innovations expand mitochondrial proteomes in kinetoplastids.

abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Plants of the genus Woodwardia have a long history of medicinal use in China. Among these plants, Woodwardia japonica, Woodwardia unigemmata, and Woodwardia prolifera are the primary source species of Guan Zhong, a traditional Chinese medicine. However, because of morphological similarity among their dried herbal materials and limited availability of organellar (mitochondrial and chloroplast) genomic data, research on species identification, molecular evolution, and phylogeny has been impeded.
METHODS: Organelle genomes of the three Woodwardia species were sequenced and assembled using the second- and third-generation sequencing technologies. In-depth analyses were conducted, including protein-coding genes (PCGs) presence/absence, non-synonymous/synonymous mutation ratios (Ka/Ks), codon usage bias, repeat sequence identification, RNA editing site prediction, synteny and mitochondrial-chloroplast homologous fragment (MTPT) identification, and molecular identification via mVISTA and nucleotide diversity. Finally, we employed both maximum likelihood (ML) and Bayesian (BI) methods, based on single-copy orthologous genes and secondary calibrations, to infer phylogenetic relationships and divergence times among Woodwardia and related ferns.
RESULTS: The mitochondrial genomes of the three Woodwardia species exhibited notable differences in genome size and characteristics; while the chloroplast genomes were relatively conserved and highly similar. Phylogenetic and divergence time analyses indicated that W. unigemmata and W. prolifera are more closely related and diverged more recently. Integrated analyses of highly variable regions and phylogenetic revealed that the intergenic spacer rrn16-rps12_exon2 or rps12_exon2-rrn16 could effectively differentiate the three Guan Zhong-related Woodwardia species, suggesting their potential utility as reliable DNA barcodes for identifying medicinal materials.
DISCUSSION: The results provide comprehensive insights and reliable, detailed organelle genomic data for the phylogeny and molecular identification of W. japonica, W. unigemmata, and W. prolifera.

title: Comparative organelle genome analysis of three medicinal species of the genus Woodwardia (Blechnaceae): new insights into the phylogeny and molecular identification.

abstract: Mutations in isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) are frequently observed in several aggressive malignancies, including gliomas, chondrosarcomas, and acute myeloid leukemia. Mutant IDH enzymes exhibit neomorphic activity that produces the oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate (D-2-HG), leading to widespread DNA and histone hypermethylation. This aberrant epigenetic state remodels chromatin accessibility, thereby compromising both DNA repair and replication. However, the mechanisms underlying IDH mutation-induced DNA replication stress and the therapeutic potential of this vulnerability remain elusive. Through a whole-genome CRISPR screen, we defined differential genetic dependencies between IDH1 wild-type and mutant cells. We identified the G2/M checkpoint kinase PKMYT1 as a selective survival factor for IDH1-mutated cells. Pharmacologic or genetic inhibition of PKMYT1 profoundly suppresses the growth of IDH1-mutated tumor cells in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistically, IDH1-mutated cancer cells exhibit profound replication stress, characterized by reduced nucleotide incorporation, slowed replication fork progression, and delayed S-phase entry. D-2-HG elevates H3K9 trimethylation by inhibiting KDM4A, thereby impeding DNA replication initiation and fork progression. PKMYT1 blockade alters cell cycle timing, forcing unscheduled mitotic entry with incompletely replicated genomes, resulting in elevated DNA damage and mitotic catastrophe. Collectively, our findings demonstrate a mechanistic link between IDH1-driven epigenetic dysregulation, replication stress, and heightened reliance on the G2/M checkpoint. Our findings propose PKMYT1 inhibition as a therapeutic strategy that exploits the intrinsic replication deficiency of IDH1-mutant glioma.

title: Genome-wide CRISPR screen identifies PKMYT1 inhibition as a synthetic lethal vulnerability in IDH1-mutant glioma.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Programmable messenger RNA (mRNA) platforms can encode tumor antigens or immunomodulators, enabling coordinated antigen delivery and immune modulation. Yet the literature spans cancer vaccination, delivery engineering, immune biology, and adjacent infectious-disease research, making its structure and evidentiary boundaries difficult to discern. We mapped this cross-domain corpus to clarify its development, organization, and relevance to cancer-associated immune escape.
METHODS: We searched the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) and Scopus on July 29, 2026, for English-language Articles and Reviews published since 2006. The strategy combined programmable or therapeutic mRNA, cancer, and immune-escape-related concepts. R-based analyses summarized the number of publications (NP), total citations (TC), and collaboration patterns; BERTopic modeled titles and abstracts after entity-aware preprocessing. Independent two-author review supported the five topic labels and characterized the outliers, and robustness was assessed across alternative clustering configurations.
RESULTS: The dataset comprised 756 publications (NP = 756). Annual output increased more than fourfold in 2021 and reached NP = 182 in 2025. China (NP = 291; 38.49%) and the United States (NP = 146; 19.31%) accounted for nearly 58% of corresponding-author publications. Sichuan University and Frontiers in Immunology ranked first in institutional and journal output, respectively. Nature had the highest retained source-record citation total (TC = 2,326). BERTopic assigned 745 publications to five topics, while 11 of 756 records remained outliers (1.46%). The topics represented mRNA delivery and immunomodulatory cancer-vaccine research (52.1%), SARS-CoV-2 vaccination in oncology and immunotherapy settings (23.6%), therapeutic mRNA cancer-vaccine platforms (13.3%), tumor-antigen discovery and immune-subtype stratification (8.6%), and mRNA-vaccine immunogenicity during autoimmune immunosuppression (2.4%).
CONCLUSIONS: Publication activity in the retrieved cross-domain corpus expanded rapidly after 2020. The corpus included both direct cancer-mRNA research and adjacent platform or immune-response literature. By distinguishing these components and identifying thematic connections among delivery, antigen selection, immune context, and collaboration, the analysis provides an evidence-navigation framework for prioritizing systematic reviews, mechanistic studies, and clinical evaluation. The map does not itself establish therapeutic efficacy.

abstract: Myocardin (MYOCD) is the principal trigger-switch for vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) growth arrest and the cyto-contractile program of differentiation. While much is known about MYOCD-dependent VSMC differentiation, limited information exists as to its transcriptional regulation. Here, we report moderate mRNA expression of Myeloid Ecotropic viral Integration Site 1 ( MEIS1 ) in both human and mouse VSMCs. MEIS1 mRNA is reduced in parallel with myocardin mRNA and protein under conditions of VSMC de-differentiation. Loss- and gain-of- Meis1 expression studies in cultured human VSMCs and the mouse carotid artery support MEIS1 as an activator of myocardin and VSMC differentiation. CRISPR-mediated knockout of the endogenous Meis1 gene in vitro and elicited lower levels of VSMC contractile markers and an increase in growth rate. Similarly, Femoral artery wire injury, in mice lacking Meis1 showed and increased of neointima formation. Mechanistically, we identified a conserved MEIS1 response element in the proximal promoter of myocardin, that appears to contribute to the promoter activity, suggesting a potential regulatory interaction. These results suggest a previously unrecognized role for the homeodomain protein MEIS1 in the activation of myocardin and the quiescent, VSMC differentiated state.

abstract: CRISPR/Cas12a diagnostics have greatly advanced nucleic acid testing, yet their extension to non-nucleic acid targets remains constrained by the intricate preamplification process and by inefficient signal transduction. Herein, we present a non-nucleic acid detection platform that integrates a CRISPR/Cas12a positive-feedback cascade with a single-atom nanozyme. In this strategy, cleavage of the designed double-clasp transition probe (DCTP) activates additional Cas12a ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes, enabling cascade signal amplification without a preamplification treatment. Meanwhile, the created single-atom Pt-engineered PdCeB nanozyme (Pt1/PdCeB SAN) functions as an efficient electrochemiluminescence (ECL) nanolabel in the luminol/O2 system, converting dissolved oxygen (O2) into reactive oxygen species (ROS) to produce a robust ECL response without an external coreactant. Using human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) as a clinically relevant non-nucleic acid target, the DCTP-driven Cas12a positive-feedback system shortened the cleavage time from 33 min in the conventional Cas12a system to 18 min and achieved a wide linear range from 10-3 to 104 ng/mL, with a low detection limit of 0.513 pg/mL. Furthermore, preliminary analysis of 31 clinical serum samples supported the feasibility of the strategy for quantitative serum HER2 (sHER2) determination, although validation in larger independent cohorts is required.
